performers: Francis Poulenc and Jacques Février, piano four hands
intro: Satie’s Trois morceaux en forme de poire for piano four hands contains seven pieces: two opening pieces and two closing pieces frame the three numbered ones. Francis Poulenc and Jacques Février play it at one piano.

sections.label: F · En plus, for piano four hands
G · Redite, for piano four hands

cues.title: Manière de commencement
cues.text: A winding melody moves above a recurring bass note and chord. Satie called this opening “a way of beginning”, and the score identifies it as a Gnossienne taken from his music for Le Fils des étoiles.
cues.evidence: Rouart, Lerolle score, plate R.L. & Cie. 9799, Salabert reprint, pp. 2–3: Manière de commencement; the footnote on p. 3 identifies the earlier Gnossienne. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/22763
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The seven headings
cues.text: The work has seven pieces under its title of three. Two introductory pieces come before the numbered I, II and III. After them come En plus and Redite, meaning an extra and a repetition.
cues.evidence: The seven headings appear in the printed score and in Satie’s autograph title, dated September 1903. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/22763; https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb44003526t

cues.title: Prolongation du même, march
cues.text: Prolongation du même means “more of the same”. The marking is now Au pas, at walking pace, and the music is a march drawn from Satie’s unfinished cabaret song Le Roi soleil de plomb.
cues.evidence: Score, pp. 8–9, gives Prolongation du même and Au pas. The song source is identified in the work’s movement-by-movement account, drawing on Steven Moore Whiting’s Satie the Bohemian. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/22763; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trois_Morceaux_en_forme_de_poire
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piece I, Lentement
cues.text: Piece I follows, marked Lentement. A long right-hand phrase runs over repeated chords, and loud chords break into the line.
cues.evidence: Score, pp. 10–11: Piece I, Lentement; the sustained melody and recurring accompaniment are interrupted by fortissimo chords. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/22763
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piece II, two cabaret songs
cues.text: Piece II brings back the march. Its outer sections borrow Impérial-Napoléon; the slower middle uses Le Veuf, “The Widower”.
cues.evidence: Score, pp. 12–17: Enlevé, De moitié, then Premier temps. The movement’s two song sources are documented in the work account, drawing on Whiting, Satie the Bohemian. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/22763; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trois_Morceaux_en_forme_de_poire
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “Recommendations”, 6 November 1903
cues.text: On 6 November 1903 Satie added “Recommendations” to the manuscript, in red ink after the music: “I am at a prestigious turning point in the History of My Life.” He signed them Erik Satie.
cues.evidence: BnF catalogue of the autograph, RES-218, transcribes the red-ink Recommendations on p. 30, signed Erik Satie, 6 November 1903. The quotation is our translation. https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb44003526t

cues.title: Piece III, Brutal and expressif
cues.text: Piece III opens with the marking Brutal. Pairs of loud chords, separated by rests, alternate with a softer melody marked expressif. Both pianists change character within a few lines.
cues.evidence: Score, pp. 18–19: Brutal, forte chord pairs and rests, followed by piano and expressif. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/22763
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Supplement: En plus
cues.text: After the numbered pieces, Satie added En plus. It is marked Calme. The melody begins with a note held across three bars before it moves on.
cues.evidence: Score, pp. 26–27: En plus, Calme; the upper part sustains its opening notes through three bars. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/22763
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Redite, closing piece
cues.text: Redite comes last. In the upper part a short three-beat figure repeats before a melody marked bien chanté, well sung. Near the end both parts make a crescendo to fortissimo, and the final chord is marked piano in the upper part and pianissimo in the lower.
cues.evidence: Score, pp. 30–31: Redite, 3/4, the upper part’s repeated opening and bien chanté melody, a crescendo to fortissimo near the end, then a quiet close: piano in the upper part, pianissimo in the lower. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/22763
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Composer of the Gymnopédies, who asked pianists to prepare for 840 repetitions with ‘serious immobilities’.
facts: Paris Conservatoire; returned to study at the Schola Cantorum in 1905, aged thirty-nine
Honfleur, then Montmartre; a room in Arcueil from 1898 until his death
Cocteau, Picasso and Massine for Parade; Picabia and René Clair for Relâche
Piano miniatures, songs, ballets, Socrate and the comic Memoirs of an Amnesiac
composer.background:
In April 1912 Erik Satie told the readers of the Revue musicale S.I.M. that he preferred measuring sounds to hearing them. He reported the results of his equipment. A B♭ examined through a phonoscope was so repulsive that he called his servant to look at it; an ordinary F♯, emitted by a large tenor, weighed ninety-three kilograms. “I get more pleasure from measuring a sound than from hearing it,” he wrote. The essay belonged to his Memoirs of an Amnesiac.

He was born in Honfleur in 1866, the son of a French shipping broker and an English mother of Scottish descent. After she died in 1872, he and his brother returned from Paris to their paternal grandparents in Normandy. A local organist, Gustave Vinot, taught him music and introduced him to plainchant. Back in Paris, Satie entered the Conservatoire in 1879. Two periods of study there produced poor reports and no diploma.
